title: Learning Randomized Reductions

claims.claim: The paper formalizes randomized self-reduction learning and provides sample-complexity analysis under correlated sampling (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook verified Definitions 4.1/4.3/4.5 and Claims A.1/A.2 exist in the PDF via text extraction, but the experimental verification was only on a 4-element finite modular addition model (Z_4), which the logbook itself admits 'does not replace full general symbolic proof.' This is a simplified model checking structural mechanics, not a full reproduction of the sample-complexity analysis.
claims.target_claim: Audit Definitions 4.1, 4.3, and 4.5 and Claims A.1–A.2 to verify the formal correlated-sampling RSR-learning framework and stated sample-complexity relationships.

claims.claim: RSR-Bench contains 80 benchmark functions for evaluating randomized self-reduction discovery (Section 5).
claims.evidence: AST parsing of two evaluation scripts extracted exactly 40 base + 40 extended benchmark registrations (IDs 1-80), reconciled one-to-one with 80 primary CSV rows. Benchmark 33 confirmed as sigmoid. This is concrete computational evidence that RSR-Bench contains exactly 80 functions.
claims.target_claim: Recount the released benchmark definitions and immutable CSV rows to verify that RSR-Bench contains exactly 80 distinct functions.

claims.claim: Vanilla Bitween discovers randomized self-reductions for 43 of 80 RSR-Bench functions, including the first known sigmoid reduction (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Recomputation from the released CSV confirmed 43/80 benchmarks with at least 1 verified RSR (87 total RSRs, mean runtime 4.791s). The sigmoid reduction identity was independently verified via SymPy symbolic simplification (diff=0). The 'first known' historical priority was not independently verified, but the core quantitative and mathematical claims are supported by concrete evidence.
claims.target_claim: Aggregate the released per-function results and symbolically check the sigmoid identity to verify Vanilla Bitween coverage of 43/80 and its sigmoid reduction.

claims.claim: Agentic Bitween discovers randomized self-reductions for 64 of 80 RSR-Bench functions by letting LLM agents propose query functions beyond the fixed prior query set (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Recomputation from the released CSV confirmed 64/80 benchmarks with at least 1 verified RSR (793 total RSRs). Novel query function 'x+log(k)' was extracted from released agentic output columns, confirming that agents proposed queries beyond the fixed prior set {x+r, x-r, x·r, x, r}. No live LLM re-run was performed, but the quantitative claim and the 'beyond fixed prior' mechanism are both supported.
claims.target_claim: Aggregate the released Claude-Opus Agentic Bitween rows and inspect novel-query outputs to verify coverage of 64/80 using queries beyond the fixed prior set.

claims.claim: On nonlinear invariant benchmarks, the regression backend outperforms the MILP backend in sample count and runtime (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Source audit with specific section references and numbers shows the LR vs MILP comparison (594 vs 1,095 samples; 130.53s vs 187.47s) is in Section 5.3.1 on RSR-Bench, not on nonlinear invariant benchmarks. NLA-DigBench (Section 5.3.2) compares Bitween against DIG/SymInfer, not MILP. Table 2 in both v1 and v5 does not contain this comparison. The claim's attribution to 'nonlinear invariant benchmarks' and 'Table 2' is contradicted by concrete evidence.
claims.target_claim: Test the exact nonlinear-invariant LR-versus-MILP sample/runtime claim against pinned v1/v5 tables and released artifacts; the expected outcome is falsification of the claim as worded.
